title: Four questions that decide a site
summary: Every idea in this phase collapses into four questions about a site: is the cycle with me, will demand absorb what I build, can I legally own and build it, and can I control it cheaply until I know. This checkpoint lesson rebuilds the phase around those questions and shows how a single wrong answer can sink an otherwise good project.
body:
A site is not a good deal because it is cheap or well located. It is a good deal when four answers line up at once: the cycle, the demand, the legal right to build, and your control over the land while you find out.

Recall

Q. What is the practical difference between an option and a conditional purchase agreement?

A. An option gives you the right, but not the obligation, to buy; you can walk away for any reason and lose only the option fee. A conditional purchase binds both sides, and you can only escape if a named condition fails.

Q. What is the zoning envelope?

A. The three-dimensional limit the zoning allows as of right: height, density, setbacks, lot coverage and use. Anything outside it needs a variance, a rezoning or a negotiated agreement.

Q. Does a letter of intent bind you?

A. Usually not on the business terms, if it says so clearly. But individual clauses such as confidentiality, exclusivity and costs can be drafted to bind, so you read every clause as if it might.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the most expensive mistakes in development are made before a single drawing exists. Once you own land, every month of delay costs interest, tax and opportunity, and every assumption you did not test becomes a fixed cost. The phase you have just finished, markets, land and approvals, is the part of the job where your money is most exposed and your information is weakest. This checkpoint pulls the seven weeks into one decision tool you can run in an hour on any site.

Question one: is the cycle with me?

Plain English first. Property values move with the price of money. When interest rates and lenders’ appetite tighten, buyers pay less for the same income. The professional framing is the capitalisation rate, or cap rate: the ratio of a property’s net operating income (NOI), its income after operating costs but before debt, to its value. Value equals NOI divided by the cap rate.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A finished building earns NOI of 1,000,000 dollars a year. At a 5 percent cap rate it is worth 20,000,000. If the market moves to 6 percent by the time you finish, it is worth about 16,670,000. Nothing about the building changed. You lost roughly 3,330,000, about one sixth of the value, because the cycle moved while you were building.

The lesson from week 27 is not to predict the cycle. It is to ask whether the project survives a reasonable move against you. A project that only works at today’s cap rate is a bet on timing, not a development.

Question two: will demand absorb what I build?

Absorption is the rate at which the market takes up new space: units sold or leased per month. It is the number most beginners leave vague, and it is the one that kills them, because time is money in a development.

Second worked example, hypothetical. You plan 120 condominium units and your market study says 4 sales a month. That is 30 months to sell out. If the true rate is 3 a month, it is 40 months. Ten extra months of carrying costs on, say, 8,000,000 of debt at 8 percent interest is roughly 530,000 in interest alone, before marketing, staff and tax. And competing supply, the other buildings opening near yours, is what usually lowers that rate. Week 28 taught you to write absorption as a number with a source, and to test it against what the competing projects are actually achieving.

Say that out loud now.

Questions three and four: can I build it, and can I control it?

Question three is legal. Title, from week 30, tells you who owns the land and what rights others hold over it: easements, covenants, encumbrances, and in a condominium, the declaration. Entitlements, from week 32, tell you what you may build. Highest and best use, from week 31, is the use that is legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible and most productive. The order matters: you cannot reach the most productive use if it is not legally permissible.

A hypothetical example shows how quietly title bites. A site is 30 metres wide and the zoning allows a building almost lot line to lot line. A registered utility easement, 6 metres wide, runs along one side, and nothing may be built over it. You have just lost a fifth of the width of the footprint, and with it a fifth of the floor area on every level. The zoning letter will not tell you that. Only the title search will.

Question four is about structure. Week 33 taught you to control land without owning it while you answer the first three questions: an option, a conditional purchase, or a joint venture with the landowner. The principle is simple. Spend small money to buy information before you spend large money to buy land.

Put the four together and you get the residual land value: what the land is worth to you after you subtract every cost and your required profit from the finished value. Every answer above moves that number. A wrong cap rate raises or lowers value. Slow absorption adds cost. A tight envelope cuts the floor area. A buried easement removes a footprint. That is why one wrong answer can sink an otherwise good project.

How the best do it

Large institutional developers rarely buy land outright on a first look. Their common practice is a staged investment committee: a small budget approves the right to study, a second approval releases due diligence spending, and only a third commits the land price. Each gate has named questions that must be answered in writing. A small developer can copy this exactly. Write your four questions on one page, attach the evidence for each, and refuse to release the next tranche of money until each answer is written down.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is falling in love with a site and then reverse engineering the answers to justify it. The control is the order of operations: answer the four questions with evidence before you negotiate price, and have someone who did not find the site read your answers first.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner answers question three, sees that the zoning allows a large building, and assumes questions one and two follow. Permission to build is not demand to buy. Many approved sites sit empty because the market never needed what the zoning allowed.

Six-Lens Check

Tax. How you hold the land while you study it, and whether you later sell it or build on it, can change how gains are taxed; get advice before you sign, and verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Liability. Hold an option or a contract in a single-purpose company so a failed site does not reach your other assets.

Banking. Lenders will test all four answers; give them the evidence before they ask.

Governance. Write down who can approve each money gate, and do not let one person both find and approve a site.

Estate. Land held personally without a plan can freeze on death; hold it in a vehicle with clear succession.

Exit. Know before you buy whether you will sell units, sell the building, refinance and hold, or sell the entitled land.

Callback

Back in week 2 you learned the outside view: before trusting your own forecast, ask how similar projects actually turned out. The four questions are the outside view applied to land. Absorption is a reference class. Cap rate history is a reference class. If your answers are better than every comparable project in town, the burden of proof is on you.

Recap

A site works when the cycle, the demand, the legal right to build and your control over the land all line up. Each answer moves the residual land value, so test each with evidence before you negotiate. Spend small money on information before large money on land.

Next: Ford, with Roman assisting, takes apart a developer who built a business district into the wrong part of the cycle.
checklist: Write the four site questions on one page before any price discussion
Test value at the current cap rate and at least one point worse
State absorption as units per month with a named source
List competing supply opening within your sales period
Order a title search and read every registered interest
Confirm the zoning envelope in writing with the planning authority
Choose an option or conditional structure before committing the land price
Have someone who did not find the site review the answers
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, a site is good when four answers line up. First, is the cycle with me: value is net operating income divided by the cap rate, and a one point move in cap rate can take a sixth off the value while you build. Second, will demand absorb what I build: write absorption as units per month with a source, because each extra month of selling adds interest and overhead. Third, can I legally own and build it: read title for easements and encumbrances, and confirm the zoning envelope. Fourth, can I control it cheaply while I find out: use an option or a conditional purchase so small money buys information before large money buys land. Every one of these answers moves the residual land value. If one is wrong, the project can fail even when the other three are right. Answer them in writing before you negotiate price, and have someone who did not find the site read them.
terms: Capitalisation rate — net operating income divided by value, the yield a buyer accepts for a stream of property income
Absorption — the rate at which the market takes up new space, stated as units sold or leased per month
Residual land value — what land is worth to a developer after subtracting all costs and required profit from the finished value

hostile.q: Your pro forma assumes a 5 percent exit cap rate and four sales a month. What happens to this deal if both are wrong at the same time?
hostile.a: I’ve run that case. At a 6 percent cap rate and three sales a month, the residual land value falls below the asking price, so I will not pay the asking price on those terms. My offer is an option sized to what the land is worth in the downside case, with the option period long enough to confirm absorption against the two competing projects.

role: Failure forensics, with Roman (risk and the lender’s view) assisting
title: Olympia & York: a district built into the wrong part of the cycle
summary: Olympia & York was one of the most admired developers in the world when it committed to Canary Wharf in London’s Docklands, and it was in court protection from its creditors within a few years. This lesson takes the case through seven forensic steps and finds the root cause in a site whose success depended on things the developer did not control, funded by debt that needed to be rolled over in a falling market.
body:
Olympia & York did not fail because it built a bad building. It failed because it built a whole district whose value depended on transport, demand and short-term credit it did not control, and the cycle turned before those arrived.

Recall

Q. When a landowner contributes land to a joint venture instead of selling it, what must you agree first?

A. The value credited for the land, and on what basis: as-is, or with entitlements. That number sets the landowner’s share of every future dollar, so it deserves the same rigour as a purchase price.

Q. What is a condition of approval?

A. A requirement attached to a planning permission, such as off-site road works, a contribution or a phasing limit. It often runs with the land and binds whoever builds.

Q. What does "substance over form" mean?

A. Authorities and courts may look at what a transaction actually does rather than what the documents call it. Paper alone does not change the character of a deal.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every developer eventually sees a site that is cheap because something is missing: a road, a rail line, a utility, a market that has not yet arrived. The price looks like an opportunity. Olympia & York is the clearest modern case of what happens when the missing piece arrives late and the money behind the project is short.

A note on sources. The broad facts below are well documented. I have avoided precise debt totals and dates I cannot confirm; treat the figures in the worked examples as hypothetical.

Steps 1 and 2: timeline and key decisions

Timeline. Olympia & York, the Toronto developer controlled by the Reichmann family, built a reputation on large office projects in Toronto and New York, including the World Financial Center in Manhattan. In the late 1980s it took over the Canary Wharf scheme in London’s Docklands, a former port district east of the City of London, after earlier backers withdrew. Construction proceeded on a very large scale. In the early 1990s the London office market fell into a deep slump. In 1992 Olympia & York sought court protection from its creditors in Canada, and the Canary Wharf company went into administration in the United Kingdom.

Key decisions. Three stand out. Taking on a whole new business district rather than a single building. Building at a pace far ahead of the transport capacity the district needed. And financing a large part of the group with debt that had to be renewed on a short cycle, so the company needed lenders’ confidence year after year.

Steps 3 and 4: assumptions and incentives

Assumptions. The plan assumed financial firms would move east from the traditional centre; that a major rail extension would arrive in time to make the district practical for tens of thousands of workers; and that the group’s other assets would support borrowing through any soft patch. The rail link, the Jubilee line extension, did not open until 1999, years after the crisis. Each assumption was reasonable on its own. Together, they all had to be true at the same time.

Incentives. A developer with a record of winning big bets is rewarded, by lenders and by its own culture, for thinking bigger. Lenders competed to lend to a famous name, which lowered the scrutiny each loan received. Government wanted regeneration of the Docklands and supported the scheme, but government timetables for infrastructure were not the developer’s to control.

Say that out loud now.

Steps 5 and 6: warning signs and the point of no return

Warning signs ignored. Office space was being completed across London at the same time, so competing supply was rising as demand fell. Tenants needed incentives to move to an unproven location. Transport remained the obvious weakness that every prospective tenant raised. And the group’s reliance on short-term funding meant that a loss of confidence anywhere could become a crisis everywhere.

Point of no return. In a district-scale project there is a point where the developer has spent so much on shared infrastructure and early buildings that stopping destroys more value than continuing. Once that point passed, the outcome depended on the market and on lenders, not on the developer’s choices. The forensic lesson is to know where that point is before you reach it, and to decide in advance what evidence must exist to cross it.

Step 7: root cause

The root cause was a mismatch between what the project needed and what the developer controlled. The value depended on time: time for transport, time for tenants, time for the market to recover. The funding depended on confidence that could disappear in months. When the cycle turned, time was the one thing the balance sheet could not buy.

Roman: what a lender should have asked

Roman’s view, from the lender’s chair. A lender’s first question is not "is this a good project" but "how do I get repaid, and from what". For a single stabilised building the answer is its rent. For a new district, the answer was the developer’s continued ability to borrow elsewhere, which is not a source of repayment at all; it is a hope that other lenders keep lending. When many lenders each rely on the others continuing, the risk is not in any one loan. It sits in the whole group at once, and no single credit file shows it.

The question that exposes this is simple: if no new money were available for two years, could this borrower meet every payment from the income its assets actually earn? Ask it of your own projects before a lender does. If the answer is no, your real risk is a funding risk, and it should be managed with longer terms, lower leverage and cash reserves, not with optimism about the market.

The pattern on a small project

A hypothetical version you might meet. You can buy a site for 2,000,000 that would be worth 3,500,000 once a promised road connection is built. The road is in a government plan, not under construction. You borrow 1,500,000 on an 18-month loan and begin design. If the road is 3 years late, your loan matures before the value exists, and the lender can demand repayment against a site still worth about 2,000,000 in a soft market.

A second hypothetical test. Ask what the project is worth if the missing piece never arrives. If the answer is less than your total cost, then the missing piece is not upside, it is the entire business case, and you should price and finance it that way.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is borrowing short against value that will only exist in the long run. The control is to match the term of your funding to the time the value needs, and to stress test the date the outside dependency arrives, not only whether it arrives.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner reads a government plan or a neighbour’s announcement as a fact. A plan is a statement of intent with no delivery date you can enforce. Treat it as an option you did not pay for: worth something, never worth everything.

Rule 34

Rule 34: I never let a site’s value depend on infrastructure or demand that someone else controls unless the project, and its financing, can survive that dependency arriving at least two years late.

Callback

In week 27 you learned that cycles are driven by supply, credit and interest rates, and that new supply is often decided at the top of the cycle and delivered into the bottom. Canary Wharf is that lesson at the largest scale: a decision made in a boom, delivered into a bust, and funded with credit that left when the cycle turned.

Recap

Olympia & York combined a site dependent on outside infrastructure, a market building competing supply, and short-term funding that needed constant renewal. Each risk was survivable alone. Together they produced a collapse. Match funding to the time value needs, and stress the arrival date of anything you do not control.

Next: Sage on the money, showing how every idea in this phase flows into one number, the residual land value.
checklist: List every outside dependency the site’s value relies on
Write the date each dependency is expected and who controls it
Value the site with each dependency missing
Test the financing with each dependency two years late
Match loan maturity to the time the value needs
Count competing supply that will open in your lease-up or sales period
Mark the point of no return on the schedule before you start
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 34: I never let a site’s value depend on infrastructure or demand that someone else controls unless the project, and its financing, can survive that dependency arriving at least two years late.
speak: Mr Shabazz, Olympia and York was one of the most admired developers in the world when it took on Canary Wharf in London’s Docklands. The plan needed three things it did not control: financial firms moving east, a new rail line arriving in time, and lenders renewing short-term debt year after year. In the early 1990s the London office market fell, competing towers opened, the rail extension was still years away, and in 1992 the group sought court protection from creditors. The root cause was a mismatch: the value depended on time, and the funding depended on confidence that could vanish in months. On a small project the same pattern looks like a cheap site waiting for a promised road, financed with an eighteen-month loan. Rule 34: never let a site’s value depend on something someone else controls unless the project and its financing survive that thing arriving two years late.
terms: Point of no return — the stage after which stopping a project destroys more value than finishing it
Maturity mismatch — funding that must be repaid or renewed before the asset produces the value needed to repay it
Outside dependency — a road, utility, transit line or market event that a site’s value needs but the developer cannot control

hostile.q: Your site is only worth the price you are paying if the new interchange is built. What do you do if it is three years late?
hostile.a: I have valued the site without the interchange and I’m paying close to that number, so the interchange is upside rather than the business case. The debt is sized and timed so that a three-year delay costs return, not the project: an option first, then a land loan with a term longer than the realistic delay and an interest reserve funded from equity.

title: One number carries the whole phase: residual land value
summary: Every idea from markets, land and approvals ends up in the residual land value, the most leveraged number in a development pro forma. This lesson builds one from hypothetical numbers and shows why a small change in sale price or sales pace moves the land value by a large percentage.
body:
The residual land value is the most leveraged number in development: a 5 percent change in what you can sell for can move what you can afford to pay for land by 40 percent or more. That is why land is where fortunes are made and lost.

Recall

Q. In a negotiation with a landowner, what is the question behind "what is it worth to you"?

A. Usually, "how much room is there above your first offer". The answer is your method and your evidence, not your ceiling.

Q. How does a density increase from an entitlement create value?

A. More permitted floor area means more sellable or leasable space on the same land, so the land supports a higher price, provided demand exists for the extra space.

Q. What is after-tax leakage?

A. The portion of a project’s return lost to taxes between the property and the investor’s pocket, including transfer taxes, income or gains taxes and withholding.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a landowner names a price. Your job is to know, in an hour, whether that price leaves you a real profit after every cost and every risk. The residual land value is the tool. Lenders, appraisers and experienced landowners all use versions of it, so understanding it also tells you how the other side is thinking.

It also tells you something uncomfortable about your own optimism. Because the residual is so sensitive, an enthusiastic set of assumptions can justify almost any land price. The tool is only as honest as the person filling it in, which is why this lesson spends as much time on sensitivity as on the arithmetic itself, and why a second reader should check every input before an offer goes out.

Building the residual

Plain English: start with what the finished project will sell for, take away everything it costs to build and sell it, take away the profit you need for the risk, and what is left is what the land can carry. The professional name for the finished sale value is gross development value (GDV).

Worked example one, all hypothetical, for a 100-unit condominium:

LineBasisAmount, dollars
Gross development value90,000 sellable square feet at 600 per square foot54,000,000
Hard costs110,000 gross square feet at 280 per square foot30,800,000
Soft costs15 percent of hard costs4,620,000
Finance costsinterest and fees, estimated3,000,000
Selling costs5 percent of value2,700,000
Required profit15 percent of value8,100,000
Residual land valuevalue minus everything above4,780,000

Two notes. First, the gross area is larger than the sellable area because corridors, stairs and walls cost money to build but cannot be sold. Second, a profit margin of 15 percent of value is a common commercial practice for this kind of test, not a standard; lenders and investors set their own hurdle, and you should state which convention you used.

Why the residual is so sensitive

Worked example two. Suppose prices come in 5 percent lower, at 570 per square foot. Value falls to 51,300,000. Selling costs fall slightly, to 2,565,000, and required profit falls to 7,695,000. Hard, soft and finance costs do not move. The residual becomes 51,300,000 minus 48,680,000, which is 2,620,000.

A 5 percent fall in price cut the land value by about 45 percent. That is gearing: the land is the last claim on the value, after every cost that does not fall when prices fall. The same arithmetic runs in reverse in a rising market, which is why land values rise fastest at the top of a cycle and fall fastest after it.

Say that out loud now.

Now absorption. If sales take six months longer than planned and the extra interest and overhead come to 600,000, the residual falls from 4,780,000 to 4,180,000. Nothing about the building changed. Time alone took about an eighth of the land value.

The same tool for a rental building

For a building you will hold and rent, the value line comes from income, not unit sales. Worked example three, hypothetical. A completed rental building is expected to earn stabilised net operating income (NOI) of 2,000,000 dollars a year. At a 5.5 percent cap rate its value is about 36,360,000. At 6 percent it is about 33,330,000. That difference of roughly 3,030,000 comes straight off the land value, because costs do not change with the cap rate. If your residual at 5.5 percent was 4,000,000, half a point of cap rate leaves you about 970,000 to pay for land. Same building, same costs, same rents. The cycle alone moved three quarters of the land value.

This is why a careful developer of rental property argues about the exit cap rate more than about almost any other input, and why the lender will apply its own, usually more conservative, cap rate when it sizes the loan.

Reading the phase through this one table

Every week of this phase has a line in that table. The cycle moves the price per square foot and the exit cap rate. Feasibility sets the absorption, which drives finance cost. Asset type sets the metric you value by: price per square foot for condominiums, income and cap rate for rental, and for hotels, revenue per available room. Title and site diligence can remove area or add cost. Entitlements set the gross and sellable area. And the acquisition structure decides when you pay for the land, which changes the finance line.

The discipline is to put a source next to every input. A residual with no sources is an opinion with a number attached.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick’s note for your personal balance sheet. Land is the least liquid asset most developers will ever own. It produces no income, it costs money to hold, and it is hard to sell quickly at full value. If you hold land personally or through a company you control, record it at a realistic value, not the value the business plan hopes for, and record the monthly cost of holding it as a drain on your liquidity floor. An option fee that lapses is gone. Treat it as the price of information, and never let option fees on speculative sites become a large share of your liquid net worth.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is paying today’s full residual for land, leaving no margin for the very sensitivity you just measured. The control: price your offer on the downside residual, the land value after a reasonable fall in price and a reasonable delay, and treat the base case as the reward for being right.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner adds land as a fixed cost and calculates a profit, instead of fixing the required profit and solving for the land. The first method tells you whether a given price is profitable. The second tells you the most you can pay. Only the second protects you in negotiation. It also changes your posture: you stop asking whether a price is acceptable and start explaining what the land can carry, which is a far stronger position to argue from.

Callback

In week 10 you learned the development spread: the gap between yield on cost and the market cap rate. The residual land value and the development spread are two views of one truth. If the spread is thin, the land residual is fragile, because a small rise in cap rates closes the spread and wipes out what the land could carry.

Recap

Residual land value is value minus costs minus required profit. Because land is the last claim, a small change in price, cap rate or timing moves it by a large percentage. Source every input, price your offer on the downside, and record land on your own balance sheet as the illiquid, cash-consuming asset it is.

Next: LEX on the rules, revisiting the paper that binds in title, approvals and land deals.
checklist: Build the residual by fixing required profit and solving for land
Separate gross area from sellable area
State which profit convention you used and why
Put a named source next to every input
Run the residual with price 5 percent lower
Run the residual with sales six months slower
Base the offer on the downside residual
Record held land on your balance sheet at a realistic value
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, residual land value is the most leveraged number in development. Start with what the finished project sells for, the gross development value. Take away hard costs, soft costs, finance costs, selling costs and the profit you need for the risk. What is left is what the land can carry. In a hypothetical 100-unit condominium, that left 4.78 million dollars. Drop sale prices 5 percent and the land value falls about 45 percent, because hard and finance costs do not fall when prices do. Add six months of slow sales and time alone takes another eighth. Every week of this phase feeds one line of that table: cycle, absorption, asset metric, title, entitlements and the acquisition structure. So source every input, fix your profit and solve for land, and base your offer on the downside case, not the base case.
terms: Gross development value — the total value of the finished project, whether sold or valued as an income property
Required profit — the margin a developer or investor demands for the risk of a project, set by commercial practice rather than a standard
Gearing in the residual — the effect by which small changes in value produce large percentage changes in land value because land is the last claim

hostile.q: Your residual is 4.78 million and the landowner wants 4.5. Why is your offer 3 million?
hostile.a: Because a 5 percent fall in sale price takes the residual to about 2.6 million, and six months of slower sales takes another six hundred thousand. I’m prepared to pay closer to 4.5 million if the landowner shares that risk, for example through a deferred payment tied to achieved prices, or a joint venture where the land is credited at an agreed value.

title: The paper that binds: title, approvals and land contracts
summary: Three kinds of paper decide whether a site is real: the title, the planning approvals, and the land contract you signed to control it. This checkpoint lesson revisits what each one binds, what each one leaves out, and the strict reading of deadlines and conditions that has cost buyers their sites.
body:
Land is a bundle of rights written on paper. If you misread the title, the approval or the contract, you can own a site you cannot build on, or lose a site you had already won.

Recall

Q. What is a non-disclosure agreement for, in a land deal?

A. To protect confidential information that passes between the parties during negotiation and diligence, and to say what can be used, by whom and for how long. It does not oblige either side to do the deal.

Q. Why do appeal periods matter after an approval is granted?

A. Because an approval may not be final until the period for challenge has passed. Building on an approval that is later overturned is one of the most expensive mistakes in the business.

Q. What are the classic elements needed to form a binding contract in common law systems?

A. Offer, acceptance, consideration, which is something of value exchanged, an intention to create legal relations, and terms certain enough to enforce.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the market lessons tell you whether a site is worth having. The rules tell you whether you actually have it. Everything in this lesson is a concept to understand and a question to put to a lawyer; property law varies by jurisdiction, and none of it should be applied to a real deal without advice. Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer licensed where the land sits.

Title: what the register says, and what it does not

Plain English: the title tells you who owns the land and what rights other people hold over it. The professional framing is a register of interests: ownership, mortgages, easements, which are rights to use part of the land for a purpose such as a pipe or a path, covenants restricting use, and other encumbrances.

The rules worth remembering are about what the register leaves out. Depending on the system, some interests bind the land without appearing on title: certain leases, rights acquired by long use, unpaid taxes or utility charges, and claims by people in possession. A survey can reveal what the register cannot, such as a neighbour’s wall built over the line. Title insurance transfers some of these risks to an insurer for a premium, but every policy has exclusions and exceptions, and what it excludes is exactly what you must check yourself.

Worked example one, hypothetical. You plan an apart-hotel, a building of serviced apartments let by the night, on a site that is part of an existing condominium corporation. The title search is clean. But the condominium declaration, the document that governs the corporation, prohibits rentals shorter than a set number of days. The use your whole business plan relied on is barred by a document you did not read. The register told you who owned the units. It did not tell you what the owners had agreed to forbid.

Approvals: they run with the land, and so do their conditions

A planning approval generally attaches to the land, not to the person who obtained it. That is good news when you buy an approved site and bad news when you inherit its conditions. Conditions of approval, development agreements and contributions the previous owner agreed can bind you as successor. Read the approval and every agreement registered against it before you price the land.

Finality is the other rule. Many systems allow third parties to appeal or challenge an approval within a set period. I will not state any period as fact; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. The concept is enough: until the challenge window has closed, an approval is a probability, not a certainty, and your contract should say who carries that risk.

Say that out loud now.

Land contracts: strictness is the rule

Courts in many common law systems read options strictly. An option is the seller’s promise to sell if you exercise it exactly as the document says: by the deadline, in the form required, delivered to the address named, with any payment that must accompany it. Close is not enough.

Worked example two, hypothetical. Your option expires at 5 p.m. on a Friday and requires written notice delivered to the seller’s lawyer. You email the seller directly at 4:30 p.m. The seller has had a better offer. Whether your exercise is valid is now a legal question you may lose, about a site you had controlled for a year. The control is boring and absolute: diarise every date with a margin, deliver notices exactly as the contract specifies, and keep proof of delivery.

Conditional purchases raise a different question: whose condition is it? A condition for the buyer’s benefit, such as satisfactory financing or diligence, can usually be waived by the buyer; one that protects both sides may not be. Wording such as "satisfactory to the buyer in its sole discretion" can attract arguments about whether the buyer must act honestly or reasonably in deciding. How that is treated varies; verify against the current law where the land sits.

Worked example three, hypothetical. Your contract is conditional on rezoning by a fixed date. Rezoning is approved two weeks late. Unless the contract allows an extension, the condition may have failed and either side may be free to walk, including a seller who has since found a higher price. Build the extension mechanism into the contract before you need it.

Finally, protect your interest. In many registration systems a buyer under an option or agreement can register a notice or caution against title so that later buyers or lenders are on notice. Whether and how depends on the system; ask your lawyer on the day you sign.

What the seller promises, and what you must find yourself

One more rule shapes every land deal. In many common law systems, the starting point for land is that the buyer must investigate; the seller is not obliged to volunteer every defect, though deliberately hiding one or misstating a fact is a different matter. The contract changes that starting point only to the extent it contains representations and warranties, which are statements of fact the seller stands behind, and indemnities, which are promises to pay for a defined loss.

The practical rule is to turn every assumption your residual relies on into either a fact you have verified or a statement the seller has made in the contract. Then ask how long that statement survives closing, whether its liability is capped, and whether the seller will still exist to pay. A warranty from a single-purpose company that distributes the sale proceeds the day after closing may be worth very little. Your lawyer will know the local starting point; your job is to bring the list.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating a land contract as a commercial understanding rather than a legal instrument. The control is a deal sheet for every site: each deadline, each notice requirement, each condition and whose benefit it is for, each registered protection, reviewed by your lawyer and owned by one named person on your team.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner reads the price and the closing date and skims the rest. The money in a land contract is in the deadlines, the conditions, the notice clause and the definitions. Price is usually the least ambiguous term in the document.

Callback

In week 20 you learned that a letter of intent may bind in some clauses and not in others, and that what binds depends on the words, not on the label at the top. The same discipline applies to every document in this lesson: the title, the approval and the option each bind exactly what their words say. Read the words.

Recap

Title shows registered interests but not every interest, so pair it with a survey and read what the title insurance excludes. Approvals and their conditions run with the land and are only final once challenge periods close. Options and conditions are read strictly, so diarise, deliver exactly and register your interest where the system allows.

Next: Sage on the numbers, reverse engineering a landowner’s asking price to find what must be true to pay it.
checklist: Read the full title register, not a summary
Order a survey and compare it with the title
List what the title insurance policy excludes
Read every approval condition and registered development agreement
Confirm with counsel when each approval becomes final
Diarise every option and condition date with a safety margin
Deliver notices exactly as the contract specifies and keep proof
Ask counsel whether your interest can be registered against title
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, three pieces of paper decide whether a site is real. The title register shows ownership, mortgages, easements and covenants, but not every interest: some rights bind land without appearing on it, so pair the search with a survey and read what the title insurance excludes. A condominium declaration can forbid the very use your plan needs. Planning approvals run with the land, and so do their conditions, and an approval may not be final until the challenge period has closed; verify that period against the primary source. Land contracts are read strictly. An option exercised a day late, or to the wrong address, can be lost. A rezoning condition met two weeks after its deadline may let a seller walk. So keep a deal sheet of every date, notice and condition, deliver exactly, and register your interest where the system allows. Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer licensed where the land sits.
terms: Easement — a right held by someone other than the owner to use part of the land for a defined purpose, such as access or a utility line
Condition of approval — a requirement attached to a planning permission that typically binds whoever later builds on the land
Exercise of an option — the formal act, done exactly as the option document requires, that turns the right to buy into a binding purchase

hostile.q: How do you know the approval you are paying for cannot be overturned after you close?
hostile.a: I don’t treat it as final until counsel confirms the challenge period has closed with no challenge filed. The purchase agreement makes a final, unappealed approval a condition of closing, with an extension mechanism if a challenge is filed, so the seller carries that risk until it is resolved.

title: Reverse engineering an asking price: what must be true to pay it
summary: Instead of asking whether a land price is too high, start from the price and work backward to the sale price, density or margin it requires. This lesson takes a hypothetical asking price of 6 million dollars and shows that paying it needs prices above the evidence, a fifth more floor area, or a thinner profit than the risk deserves.
body:
The fastest way to judge an asking price is to assume you pay it and then work backward: what sale price, what density or what profit would have to be true? If none of those things is true in the evidence, the price is a hope, not a number.

Recall

Q. What are the four questions that decide a site?

A. Is the cycle with me, will demand absorb what I build, can I legally own and build it, and can I control it cheaply while I find out.

Q. What is floor area ratio?

A. The permitted gross floor area divided by the site area. A ratio of 3 on a 10,000 square foot site allows about 30,000 square feet of gross floor area, subject to other limits such as height and setbacks.

Q. In a tax leakage calculation, why must you work from the property down to the investor’s pocket?

A. Because each layer, transfer, entity and distribution, can take its own share. A return measured before those layers overstates what the investor actually keeps.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, landowners and brokers set asking prices from hope, from a neighbour’s sale, or from a number they need. Arguing that a price is "too high" goes nowhere. Showing calmly what the price requires to be true moves the conversation to evidence, and it protects you from talking yourself into the deal. Even weeks in this course run the numbers in reverse, and this is the reverse calculation you will use most often.

The setup

All numbers are hypothetical and rounded. A landowner asks 6,000,000 dollars for a site permitted for about 90,000 square feet of sellable condominium space, inside 110,000 gross square feet. From your own cost plan you know:

  • Hard costs: 280 dollars per gross square foot, or 30,800,000.
  • Soft costs: 15 percent of hard costs, or 4,620,000.
  • Finance costs, including the land loan: 3,300,000.
  • Land closing costs: 3 percent of the price, or 180,000.
  • Selling costs: 5 percent of value. Required profit: 15 percent of value, a common commercial convention rather than a standard.

Comparable new condominium sales nearby, from recorded transactions, run between 590 and 610 dollars per sellable square foot.

Step 1: what sale price does the asking price require?

Add up every cost that does not depend on the sale price: 6,000,000 for land, 180,000 closing, 30,800,000 hard, 4,620,000 soft and 3,300,000 finance. The total is 44,900,000.

Selling costs and profit together take 20 percent of value, so these fixed costs must equal the other 80 percent. Value must therefore be 44,900,000 divided by 0.80, which is 56,125,000.

Spread over 90,000 sellable square feet, that is about 624 dollars per square foot. The best evidence tops out at 610. The asking price needs prices roughly 2 to 6 percent above anything the market has recorded, before any fall in the cycle.

Say that out loud now.

Step 2: what density does the asking price require?

Now hold the price at a well-evidenced 600 dollars per square foot and ask how much floor area would make the deal work. Work per sellable square foot.

  1. Hard cost per sellable square foot: 280 times 110 divided by 90, which is about 342.
  2. Soft cost: 15 percent of that, about 51.
  3. Selling cost and profit: 20 percent of 600, which is 120.
  4. What each sellable square foot contributes toward land and finance: 600 minus 342 minus 51 minus 120, about 86 dollars.

Land, closing and finance together come to 9,480,000. Divide by 86.44 and you need about 109,700 sellable square feet. You have 90,000. The asking price needs about 22 percent more floor area than the site is permitted to have. In plain terms: the landowner is pricing a rezoning you have not obtained and may never get.

Step 3: what profit does the asking price leave?

Last test. Pay the 6,000,000, sell at 600, and see what is left. Value is 54,000,000. Costs are 6,180,000 for land and closing, 30,800,000 hard, 4,620,000 soft, 3,300,000 finance and 2,700,000 selling, a total of 47,600,000. Profit is 6,400,000, which is about 11.9 percent of value against the 15 percent the risk requires.

So the asking price is payable only if you accept about a fifth less profit for the same risk, or pay yourself for a rezoning in advance, or bet on prices the market has not shown.

Check the answer forward

Every reverse calculation should be checked by running it forward, because a slip in a division is easy to make and hard to see. Plug 624 dollars back in. Value is 90,000 times 624, which is 56,160,000. Selling costs at 5 percent are 2,808,000. Profit at 15 percent is 8,424,000. Add the 44,900,000 of fixed costs and the total is 56,132,000, within rounding of the value. The answer holds.

Notice the units at every step. Prices are dollars per sellable square foot. Hard costs are dollars per gross square foot, which is why the gross-to-sellable ratio of 110 to 90 had to be applied before the two could be added. Mixing the two is the most common silent error in land arithmetic, and it always flatters the deal, because sellable area is the smaller number.

Then ask where the landowner’s number probably came from. Asking prices are often built from a neighbour’s sale per square foot of land, without adjusting for density, approvals or timing. If the neighbouring site sold with an approval for more floor area, its price per square foot of land tells you very little about yours. Saying so, with the arithmetic in hand, is far more persuasive than saying the price is high.

Step 4: turn the answer into an offer

At 600 dollars per square foot and the permitted density, the land carries about 7,780,000 for land plus finance. Take away 3,300,000 of finance and divide by 1.03 for closing costs, and the land is worth about 4,350,000 at full required profit. That is your number, with a method behind it.

You now have three honest structures to offer: about 4,350,000 today; the asking price, but conditional on and payable after the extra density is approved; or a base price plus a share of any sale price achieved above 610. Each one lets the landowner keep their hope while you keep your margin.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is quietly adjusting your inputs until the asking price works: a slightly higher sale price, a slightly lower contingency, a slightly faster sales pace. The control is to freeze the inputs, with their sources, before you see the asking price, and to show any change to a second reader with a written reason. If an input changes only after you have seen the asking price, treat that change with suspicion, because the timing alone tells you which way your judgement is being pulled.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner computes one answer, "the deal works at 624", and stops. The professional computes all three answers, sale price, density and margin, because each one points to a different negotiation and a different risk.

Callback

In week 17 you reverse engineered deals from public information: implied land price, rent and return. This is the same skill pointed at a live negotiation. The difference is that now the number you are testing is someone’s demand, so the output is not a curiosity; it is the script for your reply.

Recap

Start from the asking price and solve backward. In this example, 6,000,000 needed about 624 dollars per square foot against evidence of 610, or 22 percent more floor area, or a profit of 11.9 percent instead of 15. At the evidence and the permitted density, the land carries about 4,350,000. Bring that method, and three structures, to the table.

Next: JAX runs the full mock meeting, an investment committee deciding go or no-go on a site.
checklist: Freeze all cost inputs with sources before seeing the asking price
Total every cost that does not depend on sale price
Solve for the required sale price per square foot
Solve for the required floor area at an evidenced price
Solve for the profit left at the asking price
Compare each answer with recorded evidence
Turn the three answers into three structured offers
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, when a landowner names a price, assume you pay it and work backward. In a hypothetical example, an asking price of 6 million dollars plus closing, hard, soft and finance costs comes to 44.9 million. Selling costs and profit take 20 percent of value, so value must be 44.9 million divided by 0.8, about 56.1 million, or 624 dollars a square foot, while the best comparable sales stop at 610. Hold the price at 600 and solve for area instead: each sellable square foot contributes about 86 dollars to land and finance, so you need about 22 percent more floor area than the site allows. Or pay the price and accept about 11.9 percent profit instead of 15. At the evidence, the land is worth about 4.35 million. That becomes your offer, with two structured alternatives that let the landowner share the upside they are hoping for.
terms: Reverse calculation — starting from a known price or outcome and solving for the inputs that would have to be true to justify it
Contribution per square foot — the amount each sellable square foot leaves toward land and finance after construction, soft, selling costs and profit
Floor area ratio — permitted gross floor area divided by site area

hostile.q: The landowner’s broker says your 600 dollars a square foot is too conservative because the market is rising. Why should we listen to you?
hostile.a: Because 600 is inside the range of recorded sales and 624 is above all of them. If the market really is rising, my third structure pays the landowner a share of every dollar we achieve above 610, so they are paid for the rise only if it actually happens.

title: Mock meeting: the go or no-go on a site
summary: A full mock investment committee on a hypothetical site, with an equity partner, a lender’s credit officer and a planning consultant in the room. You get the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind each question, when to stay silent, and how to stay steady when the room turns against the deal.
body:
A go or no-go meeting is not a sales pitch. Your job is to show the room you have already tried hard to kill the deal yourself, and to say exactly what would make you walk away.

Recall

Q. What was the root cause of the Olympia & York collapse?

A. A mismatch between value that needed years, for transport, tenants and a market recovery, and funding that depended on lenders renewing short-term debt. When the cycle turned, the group could not buy the time it needed.

Q. In a pre-application meeting with planners, what are you mainly trying to learn?

A. What the authority will and will not support, what conditions it is likely to impose, and who decides. You listen more than you present.

Q. What is the most useful question to ask an adviser whose conclusion you doubt?

A. "What facts would change your view?" It shows you the assumptions their advice rests on without accusing them of being wrong.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the decision to commit to land is the one that most often needs other people’s money and approval. A partner, a lender or your own board will judge not only the site but you: whether you know your numbers, whether you can hear bad news, and whether you will stop when the evidence says stop. People who fund developers say, in many different ways, that they back the person who can name the reasons to say no.

The setup

This is a composite scene with hypothetical numbers. You are presenting a site for a 100-unit condominium. The landowner wants 6,000,000 dollars. Your downside residual, prices 5 percent lower and sales six months slower, supports about 3,000,000; your base case supports about 4,350,000. You propose an option at 4,350,000 with a price uplift if extra density is approved.

Around the table: Dana, an equity partner who has lost money on land before; Malik, a credit officer from the bank you hope will lend; and your planning consultant. You have ten minutes to present and as long as they like to question.

The opening: bottom line first

Say: "I’m recommending we buy an option, not the land. Base case, the site carries about 4.35 million. Downside, about 3 million. The landowner wants 6. I’m asking for approval to spend 150,000 on a 9-month option and diligence, with the right to buy at 4.35, plus an uplift only if extra density is approved. If absorption at the two competing projects falls below 3 a month during the option, I will recommend we walk."

That opening does four things: it states the decision, the money at risk now, the price logic, and the condition for walking away. Everything after is evidence.

The questions, and the question behind each

Dana asks: "Why not just pay the 6 and move fast before someone else does?" The question behind it is: "Are you disciplined, or will you chase?" Answer the real question: "Because at 6 the deal needs prices above every recorded sale, or a rezoning we don’t have. If someone else pays 6, they are taking a risk I’ve measured and declined. I’d rather lose the site than win it on those terms."

Malik asks: "What exit cap rate does your lender case use?" On a condominium, the honest answer is that there is no exit cap rate; the exit is unit sales. Say so: "This is a for-sale project, so value comes from sales per square foot, not a cap rate. Your risk is pre-sales and absorption. I’d expect you to require a pre-sale threshold before you lend on construction, and the plan assumes that." The question behind his question is whether you understand how he will be repaid.

Say that out loud now.

Your planning consultant is asked about the density uplift. Let them answer. If they say "probably", ask the follow-up yourself, in front of everyone: "What would make it a no?" Leaders who ask the hard question of their own team earn more trust than those who protect them.

Lines never to say

  • "This one can’t lose." Every deal can lose; saying so tells the room you have not looked.
  • "The market will catch up to our price." That is the asking-price argument you just rejected.
  • "The planners love it." Planners do not decide alone, and approvals can be challenged.
  • "I’m sure the bank will be flexible." Never speak for the lender in front of the lender.
  • Any number you cannot source. Say "I’ll confirm that by Friday" instead.

When to stay silent

After you state your walk-away condition, stop talking. After Dana’s hardest question, take a breath before you answer; a pause reads as thought, not weakness. And when the room starts arguing among themselves about a risk, let them. They are doing your diligence for you, and you will learn what each of them actually fears.

Worked example of the second kind of silence. Malik says: "We’d want a 50 percent pre-sale threshold." The temptation is to negotiate it on the spot. Don’t. Write it down and say: "Understood. I’ll come back with what that does to our timeline." You have learned his requirement without giving away your position.

The close

Meetings like this often end without anyone saying what was decided. Do not let that happen. In the last two minutes, say: "Let me confirm what I heard. We approve 150,000 for the option and diligence. Malik needs our pre-sale assumptions and the absorption evidence by the end of the month. Dana wants the downside case rerun at prices 10 percent lower, not 5. Our consultant will confirm in writing what would make the density application fail. I’ll circulate this note today, and we meet again in eight weeks or sooner if a kill criterion is hit."

That close turns a conversation into a record. It names each owner, each date, and the trigger for meeting early. It also quietly accepts Dana’s harder test without argument, which costs you nothing and shows that a tougher assumption does not frighten you. If the deal survives prices 10 percent lower, you are stronger for it; if it does not, you would rather know now.

Then send the note, the same day, and file it in your decision journal with what you expected to happen. Eight weeks from now you will compare the expectation with the outcome, which is how judgement improves.

Holding your state

Expect the moment when the room turns against the deal. Dana says she has seen ten of these and nine failed. Your body will want to defend. A practitioner habit that helps: before the meeting, decide in writing what outcome would be a good result, and include "a clear no" on that list. If a well-reasoned no is a win, a hostile question is information, not an attack. Slow your speech, lower your pitch slightly, and answer the question asked, not the tone.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is defending the deal instead of the decision process. The control: present your own kill criteria first, so that every challenge can be answered by pointing to a test you already set.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner fills every silence and answers questions that were not asked. Each extra sentence is a new claim the room can attack. Answer, stop, and wait.

Callback

In week 6 you learned the hostile question sequence: acknowledge, bridge, answer, and the honest "I’ll confirm by Friday". In this meeting you used all of it. Dana’s challenge was acknowledged, bridged to the evidence, and answered with the walk-away condition. The tools from the first phase are what make the numbers from this one land.

Recap

Open with the decision, the money at risk, the price logic and the condition for walking away. Answer the question behind each question. Never speak for the lender, never claim certainty, never use an unsourced number. Stay silent after your walk-away line and let the room argue. Count a clear no as a good outcome.

Next: Kema’s checkpoint for the phase, a mock interview, a recorded explanation, and the rules you will not break.
checklist: Open with the decision, the money at risk and the walk-away condition
Prepare the downside case before the base case
Write the kill criteria on the first page
Prepare the honest answer to how the lender is repaid
Ask your own team the hard question in front of the room
Never speak for the lender or the planners
Write down new requirements instead of negotiating them on the spot
Decide beforehand that a clear no is a good result
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, in a go or no-go meeting, open with the decision, not the story. I’m recommending an option, not a purchase. Base case the site carries about 4.35 million, downside about 3, the landowner wants 6. I’m asking for 150,000 for a nine-month option and diligence, and if absorption at the two competing projects falls below three a month, I’ll recommend we walk. Then answer the question behind each question. When the partner asks why not just pay 6, she is asking whether you will chase. When the credit officer asks for an exit cap rate on a condo, he is asking whether you understand how he gets repaid. Never claim a deal can’t lose, never speak for the lender, never use an unsourced number. After your walk-away line, stop talking. And decide before you walk in that a clear, well-reasoned no counts as a good result.
terms: Kill criteria — conditions, written in advance, under which you will recommend abandoning a deal
Pre-sale threshold — the share of units a construction lender requires to be sold under binding contracts before it advances funds; a commercial practice set by each lender
Decision process — the sequence of tests and approvals a deal must pass, which a strong presenter defends instead of the deal itself

hostile.q: You’ve told us the downside supports only 3 million. Why should we spend 150,000 on an option for a site you can’t afford in the downside?
hostile.a: Because the option buys nine months of evidence for 150,000, against a purchase decision worth more than 4 million. If absorption and the density application go our way, we buy at a price the base case supports; if they don’t, we’ve lost the option money and nothing else. That is the cheapest way to answer the four questions.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Checkpoint: markets, land and approvals
summary: Kema’s checkpoint for the phase on markets, land and approvals: a six-question mock interview with model answers, a three-minute recorded explanation you score yourself, and the rules you have committed to so far, read aloud and restated in your own words.
body:
A phase is learned when you can explain it under pressure, out loud, in three minutes, without notes. Today you find out whether that is true, and you write down the score.

Recall

Q. Why does a 5 percent fall in sale price cut the residual land value by much more than 5 percent?

A. Because land is the last claim on value. Construction, soft and finance costs do not fall with prices, so the whole fall lands on what the land can carry.

Q. What does an entitlement condition do to a buyer of the land?

A. It usually binds the buyer, because approvals and their conditions run with the land. You inherit the obligations along with the permission.

Q. Why should an adviser’s engagement letter state the scope of the work?

A. Because advice only covers what the adviser was asked to look at. Anything outside the stated scope is unadvised, whatever you assumed.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, reading lessons builds recognition. Recognition feels like knowledge until someone asks you a hard question in a meeting. This checkpoint moves the phase from recognition to recall, and from recall to performance. It also gives you a number, scored by you, that you can compare at the next checkpoint. Progress you can measure is progress you can manage.

The mock interview

Read each question, answer it aloud before you read the model answer, then compare. Be strict with yourself.

Question 1. A broker tells you cap rates in your market have been stable for five years, so you can assume today’s rate at exit. What is your response?

Answer: Stability in the past is not a forecast. Cap rates move with interest rates and credit, and a project takes years to finish. I test value at today’s cap rate and at least one point worse, and the project has to survive the worse case. Worked check: on 1,000,000 of net operating income, 5 percent gives 20,000,000 and 6 percent about 16,670,000, a loss of about 3,330,000.

Question 2. Your market study says 4 sales a month. How do you know that is true?

Answer: I ask what the competing projects have actually recorded, over what period, at what price points and with what incentives. Absorption is a number with a source, not an opinion, and new competing supply usually lowers it. I also cost the delay: on hypothetical debt of 8,000,000 at 8 percent, ten extra months is about 530,000 of interest alone.

Question 3. Explain residual land value in one breath.

Answer: Finished value, minus construction, soft, finance and selling costs, minus the profit the risk requires, equals what the land can carry. I fix the profit and solve for the land, never the reverse.

Question 4. The title search is clean. Are you done?

Answer: No. Some interests bind land without appearing on the register, so I need a survey, a check of any condominium declaration or registered agreements, and a reading of what the title insurance excludes. Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer licensed where the land sits.

Question 5. Why buy an option rather than the land?

Answer: Because an option lets small money buy information before large money buys land. I can confirm the zoning envelope, absorption and diligence, then buy at a price set in advance, or walk away and lose only the fee. The discipline is exercising it exactly as written: on time, in the form required, to the address named.

Question 6. What did Olympia & York teach you?

Answer: Never let a site’s value depend on infrastructure or demand I do not control unless the project and its financing survive that thing arriving two years late. Match the term of the funding to the time the value needs.

Say that out loud now.

The recorded explanation

Now the real test. Take out your phone, open the voice recorder, and record a three-minute explanation of this phase as if to a new equity partner who has never developed. Use this structure: the four questions that decide a site; the residual land value and why it is so sensitive; the paper that binds, title, approvals and land contracts; and one failure case with its prevention rule. Do not use notes. Do not restart if you stumble; stumbling is data.

Then listen back once and score yourself from 1 to 5 on each of four measures:

  1. Accuracy. Were the definitions and numbers right? A 5 has no errors; a 3 has one material slip.
  2. Structure. Did you lead with the bottom line and follow a clear order? A 5 could be written down as an outline.
  3. Composure. Was the pace steady, with pauses instead of filler? A 5 sounds like someone who has done this many times.
  4. The hard question. Did you name the biggest risk and the condition for walking away, unprompted? A 5 raises the hard point before the listener can.

Write the four scores and the date in your decision journal. A worked example of honest scoring: if you said "cap rate is income divided by price" correctly but forgot to explain why a higher cap rate means a lower value, accuracy is a 4, not a 5. If you spent the first minute on background before reaching the four questions, structure is a 3.

What to do with the scores

A score is only useful if it changes what you do next. Take your lowest of the four and act on that one alone this week. If accuracy was lowest, reread the lesson where the error came from and rebuild the definition in your own words. If structure was lowest, write the four-part outline on a card and record again tomorrow using only the card. If composure was lowest, record again at a deliberately slower pace and count the filler words on playback. If the hard question was lowest, practise opening with the risk: "The thing that kills this deal is..."

Then record once more at the end of the week and compare. A move from 3 to 4 on one measure is real progress; a perfect score on the first attempt usually means the scoring was too generous. Keep the recordings. At the next checkpoint you will hear the difference, and that difference is the most convincing evidence of growth you will ever have.

Rules I will not break

Below this lesson is the list of rules you have committed to so far, one from each failure case. Read each rule below aloud, then restate it in your own words. If you cannot restate a rule without looking, mark it and reread the lesson it came from this week. A rule you cannot say from memory will not be there when a broker is pressing you to sign.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk at a checkpoint is grading yourself on what you meant rather than what you said. The control is the recording: it does not care what you meant. Score the tape, not the intention.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner skips the recording because it feels uncomfortable, and reads the answers instead. Reading gives the feeling of mastery without the evidence. The discomfort of hearing your own voice explain a hard idea is exactly the training effect; it is the rehearsal that makes the real meeting feel familiar.

Callback

In week 5 you learned to put the bottom line first and to group ideas in threes. Listen for both on your recording. If your explanation opened with "so, basically, there are a lot of factors", you have found the habit to fix before the next checkpoint. The communication phase was not a soft skill bolted onto the money phase; it is how the money phase gets heard.

Recap

Answer the six questions aloud before reading the model answers. Record three minutes on the phase without notes, score accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question from 1 to 5, and write the scores in your journal. Then read every rule aloud and restate it.

Next: Omar, with LEX, opens the capital phase with entities: choosing the vehicle, minute books, resolutions and who can sign.
checklist: RULES_SO_FAR
head: Rules I will not break
speak: Mr Shabazz, this is the checkpoint for markets, land and approvals. Four questions decide a site: is the cycle with me, will demand absorb what I build, can I legally own and build it, and can I control it cheaply while I find out. Every answer flows into the residual land value: finished value minus costs minus required profit. Because land is the last claim, a small fall in price produces a large fall in land value, so I price my offer on the downside. Title, approvals and land contracts bind exactly what their words say, so I read every one and diarise every date. And from Olympia and York: never let a site depend on something someone else controls unless the project survives it arriving two years late. Now record three minutes without notes, score yourself one to five on accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question, and read your rules aloud.
terms: Checkpoint — a scheduled test of whether a phase can be explained and applied under pressure, not merely recognised
Self-scored recording — a timed spoken explanation you rate against fixed criteria so progress can be compared over time
Recognition versus recall — the difference between knowing an idea when you see it and producing it unprompted

hostile.q: You’ve read seven weeks on land. In one minute, why should I trust you with my capital on a site?
hostile.a: Because I won’t buy land until four questions are answered with evidence: the cycle, the demand, the right to build and my control. I price on the downside residual, not the hopeful one, I use an option so small money buys information first, and I’ve written down in advance the conditions under which I’ll walk away. If those conditions are hit, I’ll tell you before you ask.
